briefs.headline: New 'PHP2Shell' article tracks critical PHP flaws ahead of emergency patch
briefs.summary: A newly created English Wikipedia article, "PHP2Shell", documents two linked vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), reported in October 2026. This is a fast-growing new article, not the small rewrite the scout suspected: the dossier shows about 10 registered editors (not 3) and no reverts, and someone added a {{Current}} tag. According to the article text, which cites Ars Technica, BleepingComputer, Huntress, Aikido and php.net/php.announce, PHP developers rated the flaw 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and security firm watchTowr rated it 10.0. The text also says it allows arbitrary code execution, may affect PHP 5 through 8, and an emergency patch was set for 21 Oct 2026 at 14:00 UTC. Sansec is quoted as expecting mass attacks within 15 minutes of the release. Uncertain: the claim that it affects "any website" running PHP 5–8 comes from early reporting. The watchTowr 10.0 rating is cited to the php.announce post rather than to watchTowr. The infobox briefly called it "PHP4Shell". Edits are collaborative cleanup, not an edit war or vandalism. The story is only on English Wikipedia for now; I didn't check whether other languages have picked it up.

briefs.headline: PHP2Shell goes to German Wikipedia, which cites Reuters and CERT-EU on attacks and taking sites offline
briefs.summary: The PHP2Shell story (CVE-2026-109618/109619) now has a second-language article. Berghest created a German page (de rev 271505582) that is stronger than the English one in both claims and sources. It cites a CERT-EU advisory, The Hacker News, Reuters ("Cyber agency warns websites may go dark as PHP prepares critical fix") and the UK NCSC. According to the German text, Cloudflare confirmed on 21 Oct that attacks using the exploit had started. The PHP Foundation's patches cover PHP 8.2 and later only. CERT-EU advises isolating vulnerable older applications and taking them off public networks. The release was moved up from 22 Oct because details had leaked on forums. On English Wikipedia, rev 1381293677 confirms Ca changed the embargo date from "22nd November" to "22nd October at 15:00 UTC", and rev 1381293746 is a one-word wording change. The English page has had no new edits since Padgriffin's Cloudflare edit, and later German edits by Berghest and M2k are category and typo fixes. There are no reverts and no vandalism. The Reuters, NCSC and CERT-EU citations make the exploitation-before-patch claim more credible than the single X post on English Wikipedia. However, I haven't checked those sources myself. Two references are dated "2016", clearly typos. The patch time doesn't match across pages: 14:00 CEST on German Wikipedia versus 14:00 UTC earlier on English. It is still unclear whether the patch has shipped.

briefs.headline: PHP2Shell article now says code-execution claim is 'unconfirmed'; patch still pending
briefs.summary: This is an update to the English Wikipedia article "PHP2Shell" (CVE-2026-109618/109619). Since the last brief, three editors have made three small edits, with no reverts. Only one edit changes the substance. A temporary-account editor (rev 1381292512) changed the lead's claim that the flaw "allows arbitrary code execution on any website that runs PHP versions 5 through 8" to "Unconfirmed reports claim that…", saying this better matches the cited Ars Technica source. This supports the earlier brief's doubt about the "any website" wording. The other two edits are cosmetic. Strongshorts (rev 1381292142) added "(critical)" next to the 9.2 CVSS v4.0 score, and Largely Legible Layman (rev 1381291728) moved a citation outside punctuation. The page still says the emergency patch was scheduled for 21 Oct 2026 at 14:00 UTC, and none of these edits says whether it has shipped. The page has 19 edits so far and no SAME_AS links, so it still appears to exist only on English Wikipedia. Remote code execution is still unverified, and the watchTowr 10.0 rating is still cited to the php.announce post rather than to watchTowr.

briefs.headline: PHP2Shell page reports exploitation before patch, Cloudflare stopgap rules, PoCs circulating
briefs.summary: The English "PHP2Shell" article (CVE-2026-109618/109619) has received eight new edits from about five editors since the last brief, with no reverts. Two of them add claims that are more serious. A temporary-account editor (rev 1381293613) added that "PoCs, write-ups, and partial mitigations started circulating on the Internet", citing only a personal blog (jackalsyn.com). Padgriffin (rev 1381293884) then added that Cloudflare "has reported signs of early exploitation prior to public patch release" and has deployed temporary WAF rules as a stopgap. That claim is cited to an X post by Dane Knecht, not to a Cloudflare advisory. Ca (rev 1381293638) rewrote the lead to say details are embargoed "until 22nd November at 15:00 UTC" and changed "unconfirmed reports" to "unconfirmed leaks". His next edit, titled "wrong date", probably fixes that date (likely to 22 October), but its diff wouldn't load, so I can't confirm. Elsewhere, Ca added Log4Shell to See also. Another temporary account (rev 1381293882) questioned the earlier eMudhra link with a "[how related?]" tag. If the exploitation claim holds up, it would be a real escalation: attacks under way before the fix. For now it rests on one social-media post and an unreliable blog. The code-execution scope and whether the patch has shipped are still unconfirmed.

briefs.headline: PHP2Shell: article now also on Lombard Wikipedia; English page adds eMudhra link
briefs.summary: This is a small update to the PHP2Shell story (CVE-2026-109618/109619). The note's "three editors" covers edits already in the last brief. Only one English edit is new: PhotographyEdits (rev 1381293014) added a "See also" link to the eMudhra article's "2026 intermediate certificate compromise" section. The link describes that as a "high profile security incident one day earlier". That is related context, not news about PHP itself. The English lead still uses the hedged wording from rev 1381292512 ("Unconfirmed reports claim that it allows arbitrary code execution…"). I found no edit saying the emergency patch has shipped. One correction to the earlier briefs: the story is not English-only. Sciking created a stub on Lombard Wikipedia (lmo rev 1336192, about 30 minutes before this update). It's not yet linked via Wikidata/SAME_AS. It repeats the unhedged claim of arbitrary code execution on any server running PHP 5–8, plus the 9.2 vs watchTowr 10.0 ratings, citing Ars Technica, php.announce and BleepingComputer. That is a first sign of interest in other languages, but small. There are no reverts and no signs of vandalism. The code-execution scope and the patch's release status are still unconfirmed.

briefs.headline: Crumpet vandalism reverted; Clinton endorsements list page only got a citation fix

briefs.headline: Norwegian 'Viktor' name page vandalized twice, fully restored; nothing new

briefs.headline: Czech 'Operating system' article vandalized a third time by same account; reverted again

briefs.headline: India's Asian Para Games page updated live with results; tally put at 50 medals

briefs.headline: India's Asian Para Games page logs more athletics finals; routine live results editing

briefs.headline: Vandalism on Spanish Wikipedia page for Carmen Martínez-Bordiú, reverted within an hour
briefs.summary: This is not a news event. Two temporary accounts made joke edits to the Spanish Wikipedia biography of Carmen Martínez-Bordiú, Franco's granddaughter. One edit (rev 175930378) made her full name in the infobox absurdly long, adding things like "de la casa de David y San Francisco de Asís de Borbón y María Antonieta" while claiming to restore her "original" name. A second edit (175930394) changed her birthplace from the Palacio del Pardo to "China, near Madrid". The established editor Geom undid both edits within about 15 minutes (175930456, 175930462), which the scout's 'no reverts' flag missed. No dates, titles or other facts changed, there was no activity in other languages, and none of the accounts edited other pages.

Two more pages on Spanish Wikipedia joined the cluster, both hit by schoolyard vandalism from temporary accounts. On Río, ~2026-56273-60 twice added "corrida de Bennett Luo" to a photo caption (175931096, 175931135). Automoderador reverted the first and Nuria, the witch reverted the second (175931145). The scout's "no reverts" flag is wrong again, because these were manual undos and rollbacks. On Freeform, the same temporary account from earlier added its Spanish slogan translation a third time (175931189), now as italics. It looks like a good-faith edit and had not been reverted at the last event. The pages are linked only through patrollers, the vandals use different accounts, and no other language editions moved.

briefs.headline: Vandalism continues on eswiki bio of Carmelite friar Abel de Jesús, still not reverted
briefs.summary: The juvenile vandalism on the Spanish Wikipedia article about Carmelite friar Abel de Jesús has kept going. The page now has 8 edits from 4 accounts, over about 18 minutes. The new edits I read are all mockery. One swaps the infobox image for an external Google thumbnail link. Another fills the place-of-death field with a claim that he died in 3 BC and was reborn as a dung beetle. A third adds the nickname "Loncha de fuet" (a slice of cured sausage), height "tapón" ("shorty"), and a "500-day Duolingo streak (Kazakh)", and renames one of his books. The graph shows no reverts so far. All editors are temporary or throwaway accounts that haven't touched any other page, and no other language versions are involved. Nothing points to a real-world event. It looks like a group of people, possibly classmates or followers, piling onto one page.

briefs.headline: Abel de Jesús eswiki vandalism turns defamatory: fake arms-trafficking and terror-link claims
briefs.summary: The vandalism pile-on on the Spanish Wikipedia bio of Carmelite friar Abel de Jesús is still going, and it has gotten more serious. The page has 11 edits from 5 throwaway or temporary accounts in about 23 minutes. None of these accounts has edited any other page, and the graph shows no reverts. The largest new edit (rev 175930890, +1207) adds a fake lead paragraph. It calls him a "fictional character" tied to international arms trafficking and organized crime, and says he supplied weapons to real terrorist organizations. The only citation is an unrelated nursing-journal DOI. On a living person's biography, that is defamatory content, not just a joke. Another account (rev 175930878) adds an invented book praising Netanyahu, worded with the antisemitic "Masonic-Jewish" framing seen in earlier edits. One edit (rev 175930871) actually removes two earlier joke entries, the Google-thumbnail image and the "reborn as a dung beetle" death place. That looks like the vandals tidying up or competing, not a real cleanup. Nothing points to a real-world news event. The unverified housing-speculation and Israel themes may reflect an online controversy about him, but no sourced edit supports that. This needs patroller attention as a defamation risk.

briefs.headline: Vandalism burst on Spanish Wikipedia bio of Carmelite friar Abel de Jesús
briefs.summary: All four edits to the eswiki article on Abel de Jesús, a Tenerife-born Carmelite theologian and online religious commentator, are juvenile vandalism. They were made within about 8 minutes by two temporary accounts and one keyboard-mash username. The vandals changed his birth name to "Abel el Canario" and his birthplace to "su casa" (his house). They also renamed his books (e.g. "Me falta pelo", i.e. "I'm losing my hair"), wrote that his seminary was a "Masonic-Jewish" one, and added a weight of "2000 to 3963 kilos on Mercury". There are no reverts yet, no other languages involved, and none of the editors touched other pages. One repeated theme does stand out: two edits mock him as a housing speculator ("Especular con la vivienda española", "de Casas", "recaudacion de impuestos"). That could point to an online controversy or meme about him. But nothing in the edits sources it, so I treat it as unverified and most likely just mockery. Nothing here reports a real-world event.

briefs.headline: itwiki: new Ehud Ya'ari article created with a different journalist's bio; no news hook
briefs.summary: This is routine article creation on Italian Wikipedia, not news. The "Ehud Ya'ari" page was created by Stefantiz (rev 152998740, +4,076 bytes). The text is actually a biography of Eitan Haber, Rabin's aide, who died on 7 October 2020. It even names Ya'ari only as Haber's co-author on "The Year of the Dove" (1979), so it looks like a copy-paste error or the wrong title. Lulo then removed a link from the page to itself (rev 152998745). Stefantiz's follow-up edits, including adding a photo of "the journalist" on the Golan Heights, couldn't be fetched, so I can't confirm whether the content was fixed. Stefantiz's recent edits are a steady run of new Israel-related articles (Ze'ev Schiff, Noam Braslavsky, Robert Hatem, Homesh, Sa-Nur, Kadim), which fits a long-term writing project rather than a reaction to events. The second page, a new article on Ferdinand Bol's painting "Aeneas Crowning Cloanto" by a temporary account, is plain art-history work that Lulo tidied up. There are no reverts, no other languages involved, and nothing in the text that ties to current events.

briefs.headline: Routine copyediting on dewiki bio of WWI officer-writer Richard Brausewetter (d. 1916)
briefs.summary: The edits are to the German Wikipedia biography of Richard Brausewetter (1866–1916), a Prussian officer and author of World War I front reports for the Kölnische Zeitung. He died more than a century ago, so these edits can't be about a death or a current news event. Gezeitengarten undid two edits that had called his reports "kriegsverherrlichend" (glorifying war), citing "keine Wertungen im Artikel" (no value judgements in the article). The same edit also removed some wikilinks, and Gezeitengarten's next edit ("Links eingefügt") seems to have added links back. The edit by Yamato GV corrects a misread quote, changing "öffentlichen" (public) to "östlichen" (eastern) Kriegsschauplatz (theatre of war). This looks like ordinary article cleanup by several editors over about 6 hours (13 edits in the graph). It is not a news trigger. There was one wording disagreement and one revert-style restore, but no back-and-forth reverting. I didn't read the anonymous "Formulierungen optimiert" (wording improved) edit. It's still unclear why this page drew so much activity today, though a classroom, project or review effort seems likely.

The one revert was a single style disagreement with no back-and-forth, and all activity is on one page in one language, so this is collaborative editing, not an edit war or vandalism. We still don't know why the page is getting so much attention; an article-improvement or review effort is the likeliest reason.

This is one page in one language, with one revert that nobody has reversed back. There's no sign of an edit war, vandalism or a news event. Why the page is getting this much attention is still unknown; an article-improvement or review push is the likeliest reason.

briefs.headline: Vietnamese Michael Olise page: Thanh Hóa prank vandalism reverted, no new activity

briefs.headline: Vietnamese Michael Olise page restored again after third wave of prank vandalism

All of this happened on one page in one language, with no real transfer or other news behind it. Another wave is possible, since this is the third burst; the page may need protection.

briefs.headline: Vietnamese Michael Olise page vandalized again after restore; fake Vietnam birthplace stands

The edits stay on one page in one language, and no other-language pages moved. What's uncertain is the exact content of 75657911 and whether patrollers have reverted it since the last edit in the graph. The prior brief's claim that the page is clean is now out of date.

briefs.headline: Vandalism on Vietnamese Michael Olise page: fake transfer prank, reverted

One edit (75657837, "CLB mới", i.e. "new club") claimed Olise had signed for "A6-K62 Tĩnh Gia I" for "36 nem chua [fermented pork rolls] and 12 pairs of sandals" and scored a hat-trick 30 seconds after signing. The scout's "no reverts" flag is wrong: several edits were rollbacks. I didn't read two small edits (75657603, 75657819), but they fit the same pattern.

briefs.headline: Likely company whitewash of Hebrew Wikipedia's Atraf article reverted by patroller
briefs.summary: All three edits fall within about 16 minutes on the Hebrew Wikipedia article for Atraf, an Israeli LGBT dating app. They show sourced critical content being removed and then put back. Nothing here points to a new real-world event. A temporary account removed about 8.3k bytes (rev 44097212) with the comment "a few irrelevant entries – we are adapting the article for AI engines." That edit cut the Criticism and Crime sections (2009 credit-card theft, robbery and child-prostitution cases, sourced to Haaretz and Ynet) and the section on the 2021 Black Shadow hack of operator CyberServe. It also replaced the lead with brochure-style text and changed the website field to atraf.com. Registered user YAROMEGATRON then cut about 1.6k more bytes of the dating-history section as "repeated info" (rev 44097241) and added links to atraf.co.il in the lead. Patroller שיפוץ-ניק used TwinkleGlobal to restore the last good revision, calling it "massive removal without visible justification" (rev 44097258), so the net change is about zero. The "we" in the first edit summary suggests the company or someone working for it made the edit, but I can't confirm that. The graph doesn't flag the restore as a revert, though in practice it is one. Each editor has touched only this page, and no other language editions were checked.

briefs.headline: VisionQuest page: small Paladin-sentence dispute between two editors flares up again
briefs.summary: The prior brief said to check again if the Paladin sentence kept flipping, and it has. On the English VisionQuest article, Marco camino 10 removed for a second time the clause saying Paladin has met the Punisher, Werewolf by Night and Daredevil (rev 1381294759). The edit summary reads "Here we go again" and complains that the other editor restored it without explaining why. MillenniumGeneration had put the clause back with the comment "It is worth mention" (rev 1381294017). That makes two removals and one restore between the same two editors, about 20 minutes apart. It is still below the three-revert rule, and so far it is a content disagreement, not vandalism. Separately, MillenniumGeneration made a routine update (rev 1381294666): it renames the Human Torch entry to "J.I.M. / Synthetic Man" and credits Phineas Horton as his creator, sourced to a Polygon explainer dated Oct 20, 2026. This is ordinary fan upkeep of an airing show, not a real-world news event. Only one page and one language are involved. I'm calling it a low-level edit war to watch, not a news story. If the clause goes back in again, a talk-page discussion or page protection would be the next thing to look for.

briefs.headline: VisionQuest (Marvel series) page: routine episode upkeep, one minor content revert
briefs.summary: The English article for the Marvel series VisionQuest is getting the usual fan upkeep you'd expect while a show is airing. Editors are updating episode plot summaries and cast and character notes. The single revert is a small content disagreement, not an edit war. MillenniumGeneration added a clause saying Paladin has met the Punisher, Werewolf by Night and Daredevil (rev 1381291785). Marco camino 10 removed it as adding nothing (rev 1381293239). MillenniumGeneration then put it back (rev 1381294017). Other edits I read are small wording and wikilink changes to the episode summaries (rev 1381292276). The 487 churn figure is many small edits added together, not one large rewrite. There's no vandalism, no other languages moving, and nothing pointing to a real-world news event beyond the show's ongoing release. If the Paladin sentence keeps going back and forth, check again.

briefs.headline: ru-wiki: new 'Niamey airport attack' page is a 2023 coup retrospective, now a redirect
briefs.summary: This is not news about a current event. A temporary account created the ru-wiki page «Нападение на аэропорт Ниамея» ("Attack on Niamey airport", rev 155731681, +4952 bytes). The text describes the July–August 2023 military coup in Niger: troops under Gen. Tchiani took Diori Hamani airport on 26–27 July 2023, and France and Italy ran evacuation flights on 1–2 August. It also covers the airspace closure on 6 August 2023. The draft looks like it was pasted from a rendered page (it even includes the "From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia" header line). About 6.5 minutes later a second temporary account replaced it with a redirect to «Захват международного аэропорта в Ниамее» (rev 155731778, −4860). An experienced editor then made a −1 byte fix that, judging by its size and edit comment, removes the stray brace in the redirect (I didn't read that diff). The 9,813 bytes the scout saw are just this create-then-redirect cycle: no new event was described, and no other languages or pages moved. Uncertainty: the redirect target isn't in the graph, so I can't confirm that it exists or has recent edits. I also can't rule out a current Niamey airport incident that someone mislabelled; nothing in these diffs suggests one.
